prompt: Whose definition of quality is "conformance to requirements"?

choices.text: W. Edwards Deming, who argued for building quality into the process
choices.why: Deming argued about process; the phrase is Crosby’s.

choices.text: Philip Crosby
choices.why: Right: in 1979, writing about manufacturing.

choices.text: Joseph Juran, in his handbook
choices.why: Juran’s is fitness for use, from 1951.

choices.text: Gerald Weinberg
choices.why: Weinberg’s is value to some person.

prompt: `tickets.py` conforms to one reading of "over-60s" and still overcharges a sixty-year-old. What does that show about conformance as a definition?

choices.text: It only applies to manufacturing and not to software
choices.why: Testers use it every time they compare an output with a written rule.

choices.text: It is the same thing as fitness for use
choices.why: The case shows exactly where the two part company.

choices.text: It is only as good as the requirement it conforms to
choices.why: Right: the code met the words and the words allowed the wrong thing.

choices.text: It cannot be checked
choices.why: Its great strength is that it can: the output is compared with the rule.

prompt: Weinberg defined quality as value to some person. Which question does that definition force that the others skip?

choices.text: Does the output match the written rule?
choices.why: That is conformance’s question, and the one the others already ask.

choices.text: How many defects are left in the product at release?
choices.why: A count of defects is no definition’s question here; the first sentence of the section rejects it.

choices.text: How fast is the product?
choices.why: Speed is one characteristic, which the next section splits out.

choices.text: Valuable to whom?
choices.why: Right: the customer, the accountant and the next developer value different things.

prompt: A report screen shows every sale correctly, as specified, and the accountant still exports everything to a spreadsheet to add a column the screen lacks. Which definition does the screen fail?

choices.text: Conformance to requirements
choices.why: It shows every sale as specified, so it conforms.

choices.text: None: correct output means good quality
choices.why: Correct output is conformance, one definition of three.

choices.text: All three, since it has a defect in its calculations
choices.why: Nothing says the calculations are wrong; a column is missing.

choices.text: Fitness for use, and value to the accountant
choices.why: Right: it conforms, and the person using it cannot do what they came to do.

prompt: How many characteristics does the 2023 product quality model of ISO/IEC 25010 name?

choices.text: Eight, the same as in 2011
choices.why: Eight was 2011; 2023 added safety.

choices.text: Five, the levels of maturity it defines
choices.why: Five maturity levels are CMMI’s, a process model.

choices.text: Three: conformance, fitness for use and value
choices.why: Those are three definitions of quality, not the standard’s characteristics.

choices.text: Nine
choices.why: Right: from functional suitability to safety.

prompt: Match each Cine Aurora concern to the ISO/IEC 25010 characteristic it belongs to.

pairs.left: a blind customer buying with a screen reader
sales on the night a blockbuster opens
a new price rule added without breaking the old ones
the right price for every customer

prompt: What is the ISO/IEC 25010 product model most useful for, according to this lesson?

choices.text: Certifying the company
choices.why: Certifying an organisation is ISO 9001’s business, and it is about process.

choices.text: A checklist against forgetting a characteristic
choices.why: Right: it turns "we never thought of it" into "we decided not to".

choices.text: A procedure saying how to test each characteristic
choices.why: It is a vocabulary: it says what to ask about, not how.

choices.text: Proof that every characteristic has been tested equally, for an auditor
choices.why: Equal testing is not the aim; which ones matter is a choice.

prompt: A team tests functions every sprint and leaves "non-functional testing for the big release". What does the lesson say is wrong with that?
hint: What does a customer call a forty-second seat map?

choices.text: Non-functional testing is illegal before a release
choices.why: Nothing forbids it; the problem is the opposite.

choices.text: Nothing: the other eight belong to a later course
choices.why: Testing them in depth is a later course; asking about them early belongs here.

choices.text: Functions change less often than performance
choices.why: The lesson says nothing of the sort; the issue is when the questions are asked.

choices.text: The split makes eight characteristics look like extras, which in practice go untested
choices.why: Right: "before the big release" in practice means never, and a customer does not make the distinction.

prompt: "The shop must be fast." What is wrong with it as a requirement?
hint: When would a tester be finished?

choices.text: Nobody can say what would count as failing it
choices.why: Right: "compared with what?", and no tester can say when they have finished.

choices.text: Speed is not a quality characteristic
choices.why: It is: performance efficiency.

choices.text: It belongs in the code and not in a requirement
choices.why: A quality requirement is exactly where it belongs, once it is checkable.

choices.text: A product owner may not write requirements about performance
choices.why: She is the one who should choose the numbers.

prompt: Put the four questions that make a quality requirement checkable in the order the lesson asks them.
trap: The number comes last, once the task and the conditions say what it is a number of.

prompt: Lia turns "easy to use" into "five regular customers each buy two tickets without help in under three minutes". Who should choose the five and the three?
hint: Who knows what the cinema can afford?

choices.text: Lia, since she wrote the sentence
choices.why: Her job was to make the choice visible, not to make it.

choices.text: Rafael, who will have to build the shop to meet them
choices.why: He can say what they cost; deciding is the product owner’s.

choices.text: The standard ISO/IEC 25010
choices.why: The standard names characteristics and sets no numbers.

choices.text: Joana, the product owner
choices.why: Right: the numbers are decisions, and she knows what customers put up with.

prompt: Asking what "must not lose sales" meant made Joana and Rafael disagree. What did the question achieve?

choices.text: It proved the payment provider is unreliable
choices.why: Rafael’s figure about failures is a constraint the requirement had to accept, not the point.

choices.text: It detected a defect in the payment code that had been there since launch
choices.why: Nothing had been built; this is prevention, not detection.

choices.text: It exposed the disagreement before anything was built
choices.why: Right: otherwise the first to find the difference is a customer.

choices.text: It caused a conflict that a tester should avoid
choices.why: The conflict was already there, hidden in four words.

prompt: What did Deming say inspection at the end does?

choices.text: Sorts good from bad, after the cost of the bad is paid
choices.why: Right: it does not improve quality.

choices.text: Guarantees quality
choices.why: His point was the opposite.

choices.text: Replaces the need for a process
choices.why: He argued for building quality into the process.

choices.text: Prevents defects
choices.why: At the end, the defects already exist.

prompt: Tomás reviewed `age > 60`, compared it with "over-60s" and approved it. Why did the process not catch the defect?
hint: What did the review compare with what?

choices.text: The team had no ISO 9001 certificate
choices.why: A certificate says steps exist and are followed, which they were.

choices.text: It checked code against the requirement, and nothing checked the requirement against the world
choices.why: Right: every step did what it said, and none looked where the mistake was.

choices.text: Tomás skipped the review
choices.why: The review happened; the process was followed.

choices.text: Code reviews do not work
choices.why: They catch many things; this one looked at the wrong pair.

prompt: Match each measure to what it looks at.

pairs.left: how long a change waits for a tester
how many users finish a purchase

prompt: "100% of changes were reviewed this quarter." What would make that process measure useful, by this lesson’s argument?

choices.text: Raising it above 100%
choices.why: There is nowhere to go, and a higher count would not say more.

choices.text: Nothing: a full review rate proves the process works
choices.why: It was true of `age > 60` too.

choices.text: Reporting it every week instead of every quarter
choices.why: More often is not more meaningful.

choices.text: Knowing how many defects customers found had passed a review
choices.why: Right: that joins the process measure to a product measure somebody cares about.

prompt: A CMMI level 5 supplier delivers a ticket shop that meets every written requirement, and customers abandon half of their purchases. Which statement fits this lesson?
hint: A good process makes good products more likely.

choices.text: The requirements were checkable, so nothing failed
choices.why: Checkable requirements can still be the wrong requirements.

choices.text: A mature process and conformance did not make it fit for use
choices.why: Right: process quality raises the odds, conformance is one definition, and quality in use is where it failed.

choices.text: This cannot happen at level 5
choices.why: A process can be followed perfectly while producing the wrong thing.

choices.text: The supplier conformed, so the product is of high quality, and the customers are wrong
choices.why: Conformance is one definition of three, and the customers are the "some person".
